items.title: Compound Interest in Code: The Closed Form You Should Actually Use
items.summary: Compound Interest in Code: The Closed Form You Should Actually Use If you have ever priced a savings product or modeled a recurring investment in code, you have met compound interest. The naive approach loops month by month. It works, but it is slow for long horizons and awkward when you want the balance at an arbitrary time. The closed form is one line — here is the derivation, the edge cases, and the implementation details that bite. For a principal P, a periodic rate r (annual nominal rate divided by the number of compounding periods per year n), and t years: A = P * (1 + r/n)^(n*t) P — principal (starting balance) r — annual nominal interest rate as a decimal (5% → 0.05) n — compounding periods per year (monthly → 12, daily → 365) t — time in years The loop equivalent credits interest to the balance each period, so period k+1 earns interest on the interest from period k. The exponent n*t is just the total number of periods. P = 1000, r = 0.05, n = 12, t = 5: periodic rate = 0.05 / 12 = 0.004167 periods = 12 * 5 = 60 A = 1000 * (1.004167)^60 = 1283.36 So the balance grows to about 1,283 after five years — 283 in interest, of which a portion is interest earned on earlier interest

items.title: Password Entropy: Why Length Beats Complexity Every Time
items.summary: Password Entropy: Why Length Beats Complexity Every Time Ask a developer to generate a strong password and most will reach for a jumble of symbols: P@ssw0rd! or something similarly unmemorable. The intuition is that complexity is what makes a password hard to crack. It is not. Length is. This post works through the actual math so you can stop guessing and start sizing passwords against a threat model. Password strength is measured in bits of entropy — the base-2 logarithm of the size of the space an attacker must search. For a password of length L drawn uniformly from an alphabet of N characters: H = L * log2(N) The exponent is the key. Every additional bit doubles the work of a brute-force attack. Every additional character from a 26-letter alphabet adds about log2(26) = 4.7 bits. Complexity adds a smaller alphabet boost; length multiplies it. Compare two passwords: 8 chars, all 94 printable ASCII: H = 8 * log2(94) = 8 * 6.55 = 52.4 bits 20 chars, lowercase only (26): H = 20 * log2(26) = 20 * 4.70 = 94.0 bits The long, all-lowercase passphrase has roughly 2^41 times more search space than the short "complex" one. items.title: How a 3 kB npm package installs a 330 MB terminal app
items.summary: Elpis is an agent harness for Linux, built on OpenAI's Codex. Until today it installed with a shell script. Now it also installs with npm: npm install -g elpis-cli elpis This post explains one decision: the npm package holds no binary. The Elpis terminal app is a Rust binary of about 330 MB, with a code-mode host and a sandbox helper beside it. There are two common ways to put such a program on npm. The first way puts the binary in the package, one package for each platform, and lets npm choose. Codex and esbuild do this. It works without a network after the install, but every release uploads hundreds of megabytes to npm for each platform. The second way publishes a launcher. The launcher is a small script that downloads the binary when it first runs. I chose this one. Elpis already publishes its binaries on a GitHub release with a SHA-256 file beside each of them, and the install script already reads them from there. The npm package now uses the same three files, so there is one place where a release lives. A launcher has two costs. The first run needs a network, and you must trust what it downloads. For trust, the launcher checks each file against the SHA-256 published beside it.

items.title: 250 small tools on one site, all running in the browser
items.summary: I run a small site called Joy of Tools. It has 254 tools for jobs that take about two minutes: merging a PDF, shrinking a photo, counting words, working out a loan payment. I set one rule before I wrote any of them. Whatever you add stays on your device. There is no upload and no account. Most of the technical choices followed from that rule, so this post goes through what each kind of tool runs on and where it gets awkward. Merging, splitting, rotating and adding page numbers use pdf-lib. Turning pages into images uses pdf.js. Both are fine on a phone for ordinary files. Large scans are the weak spot, because the whole file has to sit in memory and a phone browser gives up long before a laptop does. Resizing and converting images is plain canvas work. HEIC photos from an iPhone are the exception, because browsers other than Safari cannot read them, so those go through libheif first. Audio and video conversion use ffmpeg compiled to WebAssembly. It is several times slower than a server would be. I decided that was an acceptable price for the file not going anywhere. Text recognition is Tesseract running in the browser. items.title: Decompile and inspect .NET assemblies from the command line — and from an AI assistant
items.summary: Glass.NET is a free .NET decompiler built around navigation — you open an assembly and read it like your own source. But plenty of the work you do with a decompiler isn't interactive at all. You want to gate a CI job on whether a dependency changed its public surface, emit a software bill of materials for every binary you ship, or check that the NuGet package you just pulled is really what it claims to be. And increasingly you want your AI coding assistant to answer "what does this dependency actually do?" without you hand-feeding it decompiled snippets. Glass.NET 1.3.0 covers both. It adds a headless CLI — the same ICSharpCode.Decompiler engine as the UI, no window required — and glass mcp, a Model Context Protocol server that lets an AI assistant open assemblies and read decompiled C# on your behalf. items.title: Small SaaS Queue Delivery Explained: Node.js HTTPS Push or Polling Across 2 Regions
items.summary: Short answer: for a small SaaS sending shipment updates to subscribers, choose queue push when each worker already has a stable public HTTPS endpoint; choose polling when the worker is private, local, or easier to operate as a continuously running process. In both designs, commit the business result before acknowledging the message, and deduplicate by an application event ID because duplicate delivery can happen. Delivery guarantees decide this choice. Push removes the consumer loop, but it moves the recovery boundary to public webhook ingress. Polling keeps ingress private and makes local inspection less awkward, at the cost of a worker that must stay alive. Europe and US deployment labels don't alter that mechanism; the actual endpoint and worker topology do. For a bounded set of shipment subscribers with public endpoints, I would try Infrai at the queue boundary because one API key covers 295 routes across 20 modules and its contract can remain stable when the vendor behind that capability changes. items.title: Private Object Storage Uploads: User Documents with Signed Download URLs
items.summary: A customer support app changes the storage decision the moment a 4 GB screen recording arrives. Proxying those bytes through a Node.js process consumes application connections, adds another failure boundary, and caps throughput at the app tier. Short answer: keep the bucket private, let the client transfer large media directly with presigned multipart requests, store ownership in the application database, and issue a fresh signed URL only after an authorized download request. The app should control permission, not carry the payload. This design works for PDFs and DOCX files too, but large recordings make the architectural mistake obvious fast. Keep it private. Before: browser to app server to object storage. Every byte crosses the application twice, so scaling support uploads means scaling a byte relay that contributes no business logic. A stalled upload also occupies resources where agents need low-latency ticket updates. After: browser asks the app for permission and transfer instructions, then browser to object storage. items.title: React Router: Pages That Change Without Reloading
items.summary: Open a shop site and click a product. The address bar changes, the page changes, and nothing reloads. Visitors expect that smooth switch now, and it is what makes a single-page app feel finished rather than half built. Without a router, the usual workaround is a pile of state: a variable holding the current view, a switch statement rendering one component or another, and links that are really buttons wearing a disguise. It works for two pages, then starts to creak. The address bar never changes, so a visitor cannot bookmark a product, share its link, or use the back button properly. React Router closes exactly that gap, and the question is when it is worth adding. My first check is how many views the app really has. One page with a couple of panels does not need a router, and adding one just adds a dependency to keep updated. Three or more distinct views is where a router starts earning its place. Count the pages before reaching for the library. My second check is whether the URLs need to mean anything. A shop lives on shareable links: a customer sends a product page to a friend, a search engine indexes it, a visitor bookmarks it. If the address bar never changes, none of that work

items.title: One CLI command to handle EF Core entities and migrations? Let's discuss
items.summary: Honestly, whenever I add a new model to an EF Core project, I feel like I'm stuck in the same repetitive loop: create the class file, jump into DbContext to add the DbSet, run migrations add, and then run database update. Having worked with frameworks like Laravel, I really miss the speed of having one single CLI command that does it all. I opened a proposal on the official EF Core repo (#39569) to bring that kind of workflow to dotnet-ef—letting us scaffold the entity, wire up the DbSet, and sync the database in one go (via dotnet ef entity create and dotnet ef database sync). Good news is, one of the EF Core team members looked at it and moved it into their Backlog rather than closing it. They mentioned that community upvotes (👍) are what actually help push these kinds of quality-of-life features up the priority list for future releases. If you're also tired of the manual boilerplate and think a single-command workflow would save you time, feel free to check out the discussion and drop a 👍 on the GitHub issue so it gets on their radar: https://github.com/dotnet/efcore/issues/39569 Would love to hear how you guys usually handle this in your projects!

items.summary: I tried getting an AI agent to internationalize a side project and spent longer checking its diff than it would have taken me to do it myself. It did the work. It also picked the languages, decided where the language files went, and chose Simplified Chinese without asking. None of that was wrong exactly, but I had to read every changed file to find out. So I started doing it properly, and then I built a tool for it. This post is mostly the first part: the things that make i18n harder than "wrap every string in t()". The tool comes at the end. For a React app that wasn't built with translation in mind, the work looks like this, for every piece of text: Find the string in the JSX Make up a key for it Replace it with t('the_key') Add the key and the English text to en.json Get it translated into every other language file Steps 1 to 4 are tedious but easy. Step 5 is where things break, and mostly not in ways you'd notice by looking at the translated text. English has two forms: 1 item, 2 items. So you write two keys and move on. items.title: Node.js Password Reset Email API 429 Retries With Template Ownership and Resend Cooldown
items.summary: A seller cannot act on a new order if the password reset message that restores account access is trapped behind repeated sends. Standard queues are usually the simplest option for retrying failed outbound webhooks, but only when the consumer and its database writes are idempotent. FIFO is worth the extra constraint when you need duplicate suppression inside a short window; it is not a substitute for a durable idempotency key. That trade-off became obvious during a production review of a small SaaS webhook path. A delivery timed out after the provider accepted it, so the retry worker sent the same event again. The queue was doing exactly what at-least-once delivery promises. Our consumer was the part that needed a stronger contract. items.title: Day 19: The Scope of the Customization Layer and Overlay Granularity
items.summary: An ERP installed and used as it comes is close to nonexistent. The same set of definitions goes out to three companies, and one of them wants "customer" to read "dealer", the second wants three fewer fields on the order screen, and the third wants one more credit limit check before a save. The three differ by an order of magnitude in weight, but as long as all of them are expressed as code they travel the same delivery path. In the comparison in Why ERP Needs a Definition-Driven Framework, what customization looks like under a definition-driven approach is a layer of data laid over the standard definitions. That layer hangs on the company: whichever company the user enters decides which customization gets laid on top. This post covers: Which definitions can be customized, and which two never can The four overlay granularities, and why each one is what it is Both layers read only, with combining happening only at the moment of lookup Where the customization id comes from, and which end the overlay happens on The customization id is a field on the company record, and it travels with whichever company the user entered. items.title: One Line of EF Core Config Cut My Query’s Reads by 99%
items.summary: Your EF Core query is correct. It returns the right row. The column has an index. And SQL Server still reads the whole index to find one row. The cause is one EF Core default that most C# developers never think about. In this post, I will show you the problem with a real demo, the one-line fix, and a checklist to find it in your own project. TL;DR: EF Core sends C# strings as nvarchar by default. If your column is varchar, SQL Server converts the column and can scan the whole index. In my demo, one line of configuration, .IsUnicode(false), cut logical reads from 887 to 3. Here is a simple table. The Email column is VARCHAR, and it has an index. CREATE TABLE dbo.Customers ( Id INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY, Email VARCHAR(100) COLLATE SQL_Latin1_General_CP1_CI_AS NOT NULL, FullName VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL ); CREATE INDEX IX_Customers_Email ON dbo.Customers (Email); I filled it with 200,000 rows of test data. And here is a normal EF Core entity with a normal query. public class Customer { public int Id { get; set; } public string Email { get; set; } = ""; public string FullName { get; set; } = ""; } var id = await db.Customers .Where(c => c.Email == email) .Select(c => c.Id) .FirstOrDef

items.title: React Forms Need a Typed Decision Boundary
items.summary: React forms rarely fail because the input element is difficult. They fail when several parts of the product make a decision at the same time: validation says one thing, the network request says another, and the UI still has an old error on screen. I have found a useful fix in both JavaScript and TypeScript projects: give the form one typed decision boundary. The component should receive one state, decide what the user can do next, and leave network effects to a separate layer. This makes a feature feel faster because it is more predictable, even when the server is not. The usual starting point looks harmless: const [isLoading, setIsLoading] = useState(false); const [hasError, setHasError] = useState(false); const [isComplete, setIsComplete] = useState(false); After a few product requests, these booleans can describe states that should never exist. Is a completed form still loading? Should the old error stay visible while a retry runs? Can the user click submit twice while the first request is waiting? The goal are not fewer lines of state. items.title: I shipped my first iOS app. Here's what App Review taught me
items.summary: I meditated for 10 years and lost the habit when I started a business. Six reminders on my phone brought it back, so I built Unthought, a SwiftUI app that nudges you to take mindful moments through the day. An AI video coach guides each one. Review took over a week to start, then about an hour to approve. I sent a walkthrough of every screen with the submission, and I'd do it again. Notification timing was the hardest design problem. Too many nudges and people stop noticing. Video loading needed more care than I expected. It's live now, free for 7 days. items.title: Moving my portfolio from a Vite SPA to Next.js
items.summary: A while ago I ran curl against my own portfolio and got back half a kilobyte of HTML. The only visible text in it was the page title: 17 characters. My experience, my projects, the links to my articles, all of it was rendered in the browser by JavaScript. For visitors, that was fine. For a LinkedIn link preview, an ATS crawler or any bot that doesn't run JavaScript, my portfolio was an empty page called "Mehdi's Portfolio". Every route shared that one title, with no description and no Open Graph tags. The site was a React 19 SPA built with Vite, routed with react-router and deployed on Vercel, with a rewrite sending every path to index.html. I moved it to the Next.js App Router so every page ships as real HTML. This post is about the parts that turned out less simple than I expected. I gave myself a single constraint: same content, same design, pixel for pixel. If a migration "mostly looks the same", you stop noticing what broke. So before touching anything, I wrote down what the old site actually had: two routes (/ and /blog), the shared nav, cursor and footer, seven home sections with their anchors, and three blog cards. items.title: I Built My Own RSS Reader in an Afternoon, With AI Doing the Typing
items.summary: For years my RSS setup was a compromise. I never wanted to pay for a desktop reader, so I stayed on The Old Reader: a perfectly fine service, but it felt like visiting a website, because that's what it was. What I actually wanted was simple: a native Mac app, feeds stored locally, no account, no subscription, and fast enough to triage a hundred articles from the keyboard. So I stopped wishing and built it. LumenAI is a local-first RSS reader for macOS with AI summaries, taken from an empty folder to a notarizable DMG in about an hour of wall-clock time, with me as product owner and build verifier while the AI wrote the code. My pitch to the AI was one paragraph: a local RSS reader for Mac, a premium feel, and treat it like a real engineering project, with clear phases, and ask me questions before making decisions. That last sentence mattered most. Instead of a wall of code, it interviewed me: stack, what v1 includes, what it excludes, how refresh works, what "premium" means concretely. items.title: European Receipt Storage: React/Next.js Private Browser Uploads, Signed URLs, and CORS
items.summary: Short answer: for a logistics receipt system, use a backend-authorized direct browser upload with short-lived signed URLs, immutable object keys, and a storage policy that treats tenant isolation as the first constraint. React and Next.js can send the bytes directly to S3-compatible storage; the application server should decide who may create, read, replace, or delete a receipt. CORS is part of that boundary, not a substitute for authorization. The easiest architecture is the one that leaves the fewest dangerous decisions in the browser. A browser upload should carry a file and a temporary capability. It should not carry a cloud master key, choose an unrestricted object path, or decide that a receipt belongs to tenant A because a form field said so. That sounds strict because audit storage is strict. A receipt is evidence, not merely an image attached to a record. No magic. Usually, yes, when the files are large enough that routing every byte through a Next.js server adds cost and failure surface. items.title: Upgrading from .NET 8 to .NET 10: A Practical Checklist
items.summary: Why upgrade now November 10, 2026 is the end-of-support date for both .NET 8 and .NET 9. Your apps keep running after that date, but they stop receiving security patches, so every new vulnerability stays open. The target is .NET 10, the current LTS release, supported until November 2028 (Microsoft .NET Blog). The good news: for most apps on modern .NET this is a days-long job, not a months-long one. The breaking changes are targeted and documented, and most of them show up as compiler warnings. This checklist is the order I'd follow for a typical solution, plus the changes most likely to bite. Take inventory first, retarget second. Ten minutes here saves hours of guessing later. List every deployable project, test project and shared library in the solution. Find every place a version is pinned: global.json, Dockerfiles, CI pipeline SDK versions, build scripts. Check what your machine and pipeline actually resolve: dotnet --list-sdks dotnet --info Check your dependencies for outdated or abandoned packages: dotnet list package --outdated Run your test suite on the current version and save the result. items.title: C# for Beginners: Build Real Apps With Microsoft's Language
items.summary: C# is the programming language Microsoft created for building Windows apps, games, and web services. It powers Unity games, desktop software, and the ASP.NET web framework, so it is used by millions of developers around the world. If you want to build games, desktop apps, or backend services — or you want a language with a strong job market — C# is one of the safest choices you can make. How does C# work? You write C# code in Visual Studio or Visual Studio Code, and the .NET runtime compiles it and runs it on Windows, Mac, or Linux. C# is a strongly typed, object-oriented language: you define classes, create objects from them, and use methods to make them do things. The syntax is clean and readable, with curly braces and semicolons like Java and JavaScript. With .NET, you get a huge standard library, so common tasks — reading files, talking to a database, or building a web API — take very little code. C# is a good fit for beginners because it is clear and well organised. The compiler catches many mistakes before your program ever runs, which means you get helpful error messages instead of silent failures. items.title: My Mac app can't link networking code. It still went online.
items.summary: Last week I wrote about how Stillroom's build fails if the app links networking code. Stillroom is an encrypted vault for the Mac that Lis Shala and I make, and its whole promise is that it never goes online. The build check reads the compiled binary with otool and nm and refuses any socket, DNS or URL-loading call. Alex Shev left a comment under that post that I kept thinking about. A build-time boundary makes the claim checkable, he said, but pair it with a test that actually tries the network, otherwise the exception becomes the new hidden dependency. He was right, and the first run of that test proved it the same day. The build check answers one question: can Stillroom's own code reach the network? It can't. But a Mac app doesn't only run its own code. Show a PDF and PDFKit draws it. Preview a file Stillroom has no viewer for and Quick Look does. Render an email and WebKit does. Each of those can run in a helper process that macOS starts for you, with its own networking code, and none of that is in Stillroom's binary for nm to find. So "doesn't link networking code" and "never goes online" are two different claims. The second one can only be tested by running the app and watchi

items.title: Cutting a Next.js page from 854 KB to 459 KB of HTML by weighing the RSC payload
items.summary: My /projects page in Next.js 16 shipped 854 KB of HTML for a list of 49 projects. Almost all of that weight was the same few strings repeated, and in the App Router every repeat ships twice: once as HTML and once more inside the inline React Server Components payload (the self.__next_f.push scripts at the bottom of the page). Three changes took it to 459 KB: an SVG sprite for the icon on every row, JSON-LD that links to detail pages instead of copying them, and named Tailwind utilities for the row classes. A fourth stopped the page from prefetching 36 routes it didn't need. Open view-source on any App Router page and scroll to the bottom. After the HTML you will find self.__next_f.push([1,"..."]) scripts. That is the RSC payload, the serialized component tree React uses to hydrate the page and to navigate without a full reload. Every element a server component renders appears in it as data, props included. So a server component that renders an inline 49 times puts that path in the document 98 times. On my page today the payload is 261 KB of the 460 KB document. Compression hides this. The live page is 33 KB with brotli and 45 KB with gzip, because repeated strings are what compress

items.summary: Apple is shutting down its Apple Support Community forum on November 20, ending a user-to-user support platform whose history stretches back to the 1998 launch as the Apple Tech Exchange. The forum is already read-only, and Apple has not said whether the nearly three decades of community posts will be preserved or disappear when the site closes. Here's the full banner notice that's currently displayed on the website: "The Apple Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state. You can continue to find trusted guidance and support on the official Apple Support site. We want to thank the community members who have contributed their time and expertise to help others with their Apple products." Apple told MacRumors that it decided to sunset the forum after a careful evaluation of strategy and customer needs. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Building a voice-follow teleprompter on iPhone without sending audio anywhere
items.summary: A teleprompter that scrolls as you speak sounds simple: recognize speech, find the words in the script, move the text. I built that for iOS and the recognizing part was the easy part. The hard parts were making the scroll feel calm and not trusting the recognizer too much. Here is what I learned. Disclosure: this is my app, Teleprompter Offline & Private. I use Apple's speech recognition and require on-device mode. If the language has no on-device model, the app says so instead of silently falling back to a server. That choice makes the app work in Airplane Mode and means your voice never leaves the phone. The cost: some languages need the offline speech pack, downloaded once in iOS settings. The recognizer returns a stream of partial transcripts. I align them against the script with a fuzzy matcher that searches a lookahead window of 40 to 70 words past the current position. Fuzzy, because people skip words, say "gonna" for "going to", and the recognizer mishears. The scroll jerked. I spent days tuning easing curves. But unlike Granola, Yogurt is open-source, free to use, and private. Your meeting transcripts, call recordings, and summaries never leave your computer. items.title: Your UI should tell you what's going on
items.summary: I opened a budget app last month to check one number, how much I had left to spend, and I could not find it. The balance was on one screen, the spending was on another, and the budget was a third screen with a tiny progress bar I had to squint at. I knew the data was in there somewhere, the app had it, it just was not showing me. I closed it and did the math in my head instead, which is the exact moment a UI has failed at its job. I keep coming back to a line from Ben Halpern's post, ask more of your UI. The idea is simple: a UI should act like an instrument panel, showing you what is going on, live, instead of hiding the state behind taps and menus. A car dashboard does not make you open a menu to see your speed. It is just there, all the time, because the whole point of the dashboard is to tell you where you stand. I built a little budget tracker to try the idea out, nothing fancy, just a panel that shows the four things I actually check. Balance, spent this month against the budget, the next bill coming up, and whether the data is synced. Every number updates the moment something changes, so the panel is always current. items.title: From API-First to AI-Native-First: How Should We Evolve Our Software Architecture?
items.summary: For years, we have been designing software systems around APIs. We expose REST endpoints, define gRPC contracts, implement business services, establish integration patterns and build applications that consume these capabilities. The API-first approach has served us well. It has enabled distributed systems, microservices, platform engineering and ecosystem integrations. But something fundamental is changing. AI is no longer just another feature that we integrate into an application. With the emergence of AI agents, applications are increasingly expected to understand context, discover capabilities, interact with external systems and execute business tasks. This raises an interesting architectural question: Are our existing applications ready to be consumed by AI agents, or are we going to keep building custom integrations every time we introduce a new AI use case? I believe we need to start thinking about an evolution towards AI-Native-First Software Architecture. Not by abandoning API-first architecture, but by extending it. items.title: Free Currency Converter API for iOS and Android: Swift and Kotlin
items.summary: A free currency converter API is easy to call from a mobile app. Doing it well takes three more things: the app must work offline with the last known rates, it must tell the user how old those rates are, and the API key must not be inside the app binary. This guide covers all three, with working code for iOS in Swift and Android in Kotlin. The examples use the AllRatesToday rates endpoint, which returns mid-market rates for 160+ currencies, refreshed every 60 seconds. An iOS or Android app is a file the user downloads. Anything compiled into it, including an API key in Info.plist, BuildConfig or an obfuscated string, can be extracted with free tools in minutes. Once extracted, the key works from anywhere until you rotate it. So the app never talks to the rates API directly: The app calls https://rates.example.com/rates?source=USD&target=EUR,GBP,JPY on your own backend. The backend adds Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY, calls AllRatesToday, caches the answer and returns the same JSON array. items.title: How NewsNinja syncs all your data in less than 1 MB of iCloud
items.summary: NewsNinja is an RSS reader for iPhone, iPad, Mac, and Vision Pro that I build after hours. This post was originally published on the NewsNinja blog. NewsNinja has no account and no sync server, but it still syncs between your iPhone, iPad, Vision Pro, and Mac. Your feeds, categories, settings, read articles, and starred articles all go through a single, small Apple API: NSUbiquitousKeyValueStore, the iCloud key-value store. The whole thing fits in less than 1 MB. This post explains how the store works, why I picked it, and the tricks that keep NewsNinja inside its limits as the app has grown. The first version of NewsNinja was a very simple RSS reader. The only thing that needed to sync was the list of feeds you subscribed to, and a feed list is just a list of URLs. For that, a real database felt like overkill. Core Data or SwiftData would have meant a schema, a model container, migrations, and a CloudKit container to set up and maintain, all to store an array of strings. I didn't want to run my own sync server either. NewsNinja doesn't have accounts, and I wanted to keep it that way. NSUbiquitousKeyValueStore was exactly the right size for the problem. items.title: From idea to the App Store in a weekend: a medication reminder built in November 2026
items.summary: On Thursday evening at 20:40 I opened an empty folder with a short note: remind me to take my pills, let me confirm I took them, keep a history, count what is left at home. On Friday at about 16:00 the app was submitted to App Store review, for iPhone, iPad and Mac, in four languages. On Monday morning Apple approved it. The app is Vzato ("taken" in Czech), and it is in the App Store now. It is free, open source under MPL-2.0, has no server and no accounts, and syncs through the user's own iCloud. The code is on GitHub. I built it with Claude Code. This post is about what that looked like in practice: why I built it, how the day went, what I did and what the AI did, and what it means to write and ship an app like this now. It wasn't magic, and it wasn't a toy either. There are plenty of them. I tried several before this, and none of them worked for me. Some I did not like. Some I simply did not understand how to use. And most of them missed small things that matter a lot when you actually take pills every day: When can I eat? Some medication has to be taken on an empty stomach, 30 minutes before food. So the reminder I need is not only "take your pill", it is also "you can eat now"

items.summary: Point a general camera translator at a page of raw manga and you get one of two results. A single paragraph of English in an order that makes no sense, or one tiny box per column of text, each translated on its own, so nothing reads like a sentence. I build Yomi, an iOS app for reading manga that only exists in Japanese, and most of the work turned out not to be translation at all. It was geometry: deciding which pieces of text belong to the same speech bubble, in what order to read them, and where to put the English afterwards. This post is about that part. Three things a sign or a menu never does to you: Vertical text. Japanese bubbles are usually written in columns, top to bottom, and the columns read right to left. OCR engines tend to return each column as its own line. Many separate blocks. A page has eight to fifteen bubbles. A translator that treats the page as one block of text merges dialogue from different characters. Small text at page scale. A whole page photographed by a phone leaves each glyph a few pixels wide. Gaby Wood, chief executive of the Booker Prize Foundation, said that while plenty of previous winners had dabbled in science fiction, Harrison's was "the first Booker winner to have emerged from the bona fide SF world." She called it "a historic win, for a writer whose decades of work are lightly worn on every page". Harrison, who has been publishing for six decades, overtakes Margaret Atwood, who was 79 when she shared the prize in 2019 for The Testaments. He received the 50,000-pound award and trophy at a ceremony in London on Monday evening. The End of Everything, Harrison's first Booker nomination, is set a few decades from now, years after a disaster nobody can properly account for. items.title: MAI-Transcribe-2 (125 minute read)
items.summary: MAI-Transcribe-2 is the fastest, most accurate, and cheapest speech recognition model in the world. It has new features like diarization, configurable transcription styles, and word-level timestamps. MAI-Transcribe-2 can handle a broader range of real-world audio than leading models like Gemini 3.5 Transcribe, GPT-Transcribe, Whisper V3-Large, and ScribeV2. items.title: ‘Flying cars' could launch in China next summer, maker of two-seat model says (4 minute read)
items.summary: XPeng's $300,000 low-altitude flying car will be ready for use in the second half of 2027. About the size of a Fiat 500, the vehicle can fly using six drone-like battery-powered propellers. It can be steered using a joystick or fly autonomously to a programmed destination. The price tag includes a six-wheeled van for transporting the vehicle. The flying car has a flight range of 30 kilometers, but XPeng says this will soon be doubled.

items.title: Modern Web Guidance 1.0: The web platform expertise your coding agent is missing (15 minute read)
items.summary: The Modern Web Guidance is a set of skills that embed web platform expertise, best practices, and browser compatibility data directly into coding agents. The stable release of the guidance includes a new modernization workflow, an expanded guide database, deeper human expert review for every guide, and full evaluation coverage across all of the guides. Firefox and Edge have joined Chrome to support Modern Web Guidance to improve cross-browser compatibility and contribute to the project. The project aims to ensure that anyone coding with agents can take full advantage of the power and capabilities of the modern web platform.

items.title: Apple's Claris Testing 'Harbor' App for Local AI on Macs (2 minute read)
items.summary: Harbor is an app currently being tested by Apple's Claris subsidiary that turns Apple Silicon Macs into private AI servers. It supports connecting multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool unified memory and enable larger models with higher concurrency. Harbor is in early access and not publicly available. There was an App Store listing, but it has now been removed, so it isn't clear whether the app will be free. The sign-up page for the app asks for a company name, suggesting a business focus.

items.title: Fireworks AI Confirms Wider Breach Affecting Notion AI Chats
items.summary: Fireworks AI says its October breach was broader than initially disclosed, with attackers gaining access to customer account and billing information as well as some datasets, incomplete model weights and secrets. Notion, the popular productivity and note-taking app, disclosed that it was impacted in the breach but "fewer than 1% of Notion workspaces" were involved. "Upon analysis of the new data, we discovered that it included Notion AI chat transcripts used for the Insights feature, which for the vast majority of impacted workspaces were unattributable," it said. "'Unattributable' means the chats weren't labeled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from, and the transcripts did not contain tool call results." The Hacker News reports: In a notice published on October 10, 2026, [Fireworks AI] said it detected unauthorized use of internal Fireworks credentials that allowed an unauthorized third-party to access environment variables used in evaluation jobs in a limited number of customer accounts. The activity was detected on October 6, 2026, at 9 a.m. PDT. [...] The latest bulletin from the company reveals that the scope of the breach may have been broader than previously

items.title: What objective is reasoning solving? (12 minute read)
items.summary: Reasoning is pathfinding in token space. There are many paths from the problem to a correct answer, and the model traverses each of them with each sample. A path is not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer - it's only in aggregate, over the distribution of paths, do we get a high probability of success. RL training directly raises the success probability. The gains credited to 'thinking longer' come from the search paid for during training rather than at inference.

items.title: Two Kinds of Test-Time Scaling (28 minute read)
items.summary: Test-time scaling trades compute for performance at test time. There are two types of test-time scaling: one allows researchers to trade more compute for more performance per task, but only up to the maximum quantity of per-task compute used during training; and the other lets researchers trade more compute for more performance per task, and lets them do so up to quantities of compute and performance that never occurred during training. Scaling methods that permit the latter change will have a larger impact than test-time scaling considered simply. This essay describes how this may impact the world.

items.title: They Created a Cell That's Almost Alive. What to Do With It Now? (8 minute read)
items.summary: A SpudCell is an artificial cell created from lifeless ingredients that can grow, copy its DNA, divide in two, and start its cell cycle all over again. It is still far from a self-sustaining cell that any scientist could manufacture from prepared ingredients, but the technology could eventually make it easier to produce medicines, foods, and other items that could not otherwise be produced with ordinary biology. The researchers working on SpudCell hope that it will eventually be a platform for biotechnology that will allow a simple cell to be engineered in scores of useful ways. SpudCell could potentially be misused, so its researchers are taking security seriously from the start - its DNA and proteins are engineered so that it can only survive on an exotic diet of chemicals not found in nature.

Novel software is something that has fundamentally not existed before. Writing novel software with agents is challenging, as they are not trained on the task. Not a lot of software is novel, which is fine, as there is still a ton of value in the interpolative stuff.

items.summary: The author believes we are at a turning point as a species – and even in the shadow of big tech it’s up to us how we want to proceed ‘I am a storyteller by trade,” writes Jeanette Winterson on the first page of her 2021 book 12 Bytes, an idiosyncratic and thought-provoking series of essays in which she considered just how artificial intelligence might change everything about our lives. “And I know everything we do is a fiction until it’s a fact: the dream of flying, the dream of space travel, the dream of speaking to someone instantly, across time and space, the dream of not dying – or of returning.” She had already been thinking about our possible futures for at least 15 years – her 2007 novel, The Stone Gods, for instance, imagined a post-climate catastrophe world populated by robots and humans who never age, while 12 Bytes was preceded by Frankisstein: A Love Story, which alternates a recreation of the summer Mary Shelley wrote Frankenstein with a trans doctor’s travels among present-day cryogenecists and AI-enabled robots.
